# Project Overview 

[I'm someone who considers themselves an active individual. I train 6 days a week pretty much year round which includes a mixture of lifting, running, swimming, & biking. As a way to analyze my overall activity level, I decided to compile observations across several key variables to see if there were any key relationships that could be identified.]{style=font-size:"110%";}

## The outline for this analysis is as follows:

**Question:**

How does does amount of time I slept influence the amount of steps I take in a day?

**Response Variable:**

The amount of steps walked in day.

**Predictor Variable:**

The amount of time slept only a nightly basis 

**Additional Variables Measured:**

(1) Weather - If it’s particularly wet or cold out, this will influence how much time I spend
outside and therefore, how much I spend walking

(2) Schedule for the day - I don’t have many classes this quarter but the amount of in-person
meetings I have heavily fluctuates on a weekly basis. On weeks where I have a lot of
in-person meetings, I predict my step count will go up.

(3) Specific Training - I currently cross-train to prevent overuse injuries. On weeks where I
intend to run more, I predict my step count will be higher

(4) Caffeine Intake - I try not to drink caffeine heavily or rotate days that I do. However, I’m
interested to see how caffeine intake could affect step count as I normally drink caffeine
on days when I’m feeling more fatigue than usual in an attempt to reach my baseline

## Set Up 

To begin, I loaded in several R packages which will be useful for data visualization as well as proper analysis.
```{r}
#| label: set-up
#| message: false

# Reading in necessary packages 
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(janitor)
library(readxl)

# Storing personal data as specificed object 
step_count <- read_csv(
  here("data", "MyData_HW3_Format.csv"))
```


## Cleaning My Data 

Before processing any data, it's important I clean the file containing my observations to ensure proper naming schemes are set and any null values are removed.
```{r}
# cleaning my data before creating ggplot 
my_data_clean <- step_count |> 
  # cleaning names 
  clean_names() |> 
  # removing any NA values 
  filter(!is.na(day_of_the_week))
```

## Summarizing Data 

The next step is to create a summary statistics file. In this case, I'm looking to find the mean number of steps taken for each day of the week across all of my observations.
```{r}
# creating summary data to find the mean steps per each day of the week 
my_data_summary <- my_data_clean |> 
  # grouping the days of the week 
  group_by(day_of_the_week) |> 
  # calculating the mean number of steps for each day of the week
  summarise(mean_steps = mean(total_steps_taken_for_the_day)) |> 
  # ungrouping the data for good measure
  ungroup()
```

### Data Visualization #1

For my first visualization, I'm looking to identify if there were specific days of the week where mean daily step counts were highest. 
```{r}
# ggplot as base layer 
ggplot(data = my_data_summary,
       # designating x and y axis to specified columns within the dataset 
       mapping = aes(x = fct_relevel(day_of_the_week, # setting a specified order for the data to be displayed
                       "Sun", 
                       "Mon", 
                       "Tue", 
                       "Wed", 
                       "Thurs", 
                       "Fri", 
                       "Sat"), y = mean_steps)) + 
  # Adding first layer 
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue4", # each column will be blue
           color = "gray20", # each column will be outlined in black
           width = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Day of the Week", # x-axis is days of the week 
       y = "Total Daily Steps Taken", # y-axis is total daily steps taken
       title = "Average Daily Step Count by Day of the Week", # setting the title
       subtitle = "Most Reccent Observation: May 27, 2026") + # creating a subtitle
  theme_classic() + # updating theme to remove extra visuals
  # Customizing plot text and appearance 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", # bolding the title
                                  color = "gray10"), #making the title gray
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray35"), # choosing color
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"), # bolding the axes
        axis.text = element_text(color = "gray20")) # axes color
```
**Figure 1:** 

Average daily step count grouped by day of the week using observations collected over the course of the observation period. Thursday had the highest average daily step count while Sunday had the lowest average daily step count, suggesting that activity levels varied noticeably depending on the day of the week.

## Data Visualization #2: 

For my secoond visualization, I wanted to understand if there was a relationship between the duration of sleep I received each night and the total steps taken for the day.
```{r}
#creating ggplot base layer
ggplot(data = my_data_clean, 
       mapping = aes(x = duration_of_sleep_minutes,
                    y = total_steps_taken_for_the_day)) + 
  # Adding a QQ plot 
  geom_point(color = "steelblue4",
             size = 2,
             alpha = 0.7,
             shape = 21) + 
  # Adding a linear regression trendline 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              color = "gray25",
              fill = "lightblue") +
  # Adding custom labels for the x and y axis
  labs(x = "Duration of Sleep (Minutes)",
       y = "Total Daily Steps Taken",
       title = "Observing A Potential Relationship Between Total Daily Steps Taken 
For The Day & the Duration of Sleep Achieved",
      subtitle = "Most Recent Observation: May 27, 2026") + 
  # Updating the theme to remove grid lines 
  theme_classic() + 
  # Customizing the theme elements 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", # bolding the title
                                  color = "gray10"), #making the title gray
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray35"), # choosing color
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"), # bolding the axes
        axis.text = element_text(color = "gray20")) # axes color
  
```

**Figure 2:**

The relationship between sleep duration (minutes) and total daily step count across all observations collected during the study period. The fitted linear regression line suggests a slight negative relationship between sleep duration and daily activity, indicating that higher sleep durations were generally associated with lower total daily step counts.

# Findings

My findings, although initially surprising, make sense when given the broader context of my daily routine. As seen in *Figure 2*, there seems to be a negative correlation between duration of sleep (minutes) and total daily steps taken. While this may seem counter-intuitive, it makes sense given that I tend to sleep more on my *rest* days as I don't need to wake up early to workout and generally have a lighter schedule load.
